Introduction to Individual Decision-Maki: Self-test: explain why two different utility scales can represent the same preference ordering, then give one situation where the spacing between utility numbers would start to matter. If you cannot separate ranking from scale, the later payoff tables will feel more objective than they are.
Representation of Games: Self-test: take one example and say what would change if the move order were reversed or if one player could not observe an earlier action. If the answer changes, the representation is doing real modeling work rather than simply drawing the story.
Dominance: Self-test: find one action you want to delete and prove the deletion without using the word likely. If your explanation depends on what you expect the opponent to do, you are making a belief argument, not a dominance argument.
Rationalizability: Self-test: defend an action that is not your favorite prediction by constructing a belief that makes it optimal. Then state why that defense still falls short of equilibrium. This checks whether you understand survival under belief as weaker than mutual consistency.
Nash Equilibrium: Self-test: reject one tempting outcome by identifying exactly one profitable unilateral deviation. Then find one outcome where that same one-player switch test fails for every player. This separates Nash stability from efficiency or moral appeal.
Imperfect Competition: Self-test: write a sentence that begins, 'my firm's best output depends on your output because...' and finish it with demand, price, or cost. If the rival disappears from the sentence, you have slipped back into single-agent optimization.
Zero-Sum Games: Self-test: show why randomizing can protect a player from being targeted. Then name one economic setting from the course that is competitive but not zero-sum. This checks both the power and the boundary of minimax-style reasoning.
Backward Induction: Self-test: identify a threat in the lecture and solve the node where that threat would be executed. If the threatened action is not optimal there, explain how the earlier story changes. This is the core credibility move.
Negotiation: Self-test: change only one outside option or waiting cost and predict how the split should move. If your answer uses toughness without changing a continuation payoff, you have left the model and returned to informal personality language. Then state which side's threat point actually improved.
Subgame-Perfect Nash Equilibrium: Self-test: name a Nash-looking strategy profile that relies on a later threat. Then test the threat inside the subgame after the relevant history. If it fails there, explain why Nash at the start was too weak.
One-Shot Deviation Principle and Bargain: Self-test: choose one history and compare the planned action with exactly one current deviation. Then say which theorem condition makes this local check informative. If you cannot name the condition, the shortcut is being used mechanically.
Finitely Repeated Games: Self-test: write the final-round incentive first, then explain how that final answer affects the previous round. If you still predict cooperation, name the extra ingredient that blocks backward unraveling, such as reputation outside the modeled game.
Infinitely Repeated Games: Self-test: write the deviation gain on one side and the discounted punishment value on the other. Then lower the discount factor and say which side becomes harder to satisfy. This turns 'long relationship' into an incentive inequality.
Folk Theorem: Self-test: pick a payoff vector and classify it as infeasible, feasible but not individually rational, or potentially supportable. Then explain why supportable does not mean selected. This checks the theorem's central possibility-versus-prediction distinction. Add the punishment story that would make the payoff self-enforcing.
Implicit Cartels: Self-test: describe a high-price pattern twice: once as explicit agreement and once as tacit repeated-game discipline. Then list what evidence would distinguish the two. This prevents the model from being mistaken for a legal conclusion.
Bayesian Games: Self-test: rewrite a complete-information strategy as a type-contingent rule. Then identify the prior belief that lets other players reason about hidden types. If there is no type rule, the private-information structure is not yet modeled.
Bayesian Nash Equilibrium: Applications: Self-test: choose two types and check their deviations separately. If one type wants to deviate while another does not, explain why an average-player check would miss the failure. This is the applied BNE audit.
Auctions: Self-test: compare two bids by writing how each changes winning probability and surplus if winning. Then repeat after changing the payment rule. If the same bid logic survives every format, you are probably ignoring the mechanism. Name whether the bidder pays their own bid, another bid, or a platform price.
Revenue Equivalence: Self-test: take a proposed use of revenue equivalence and strike out one assumption, such as risk neutrality or symmetry. Then explain which step of the equivalence story breaks. The theorem is learned by testing its failure points. Do not call formats equivalent until the allocation rule also matches.
Ad Auctions: Self-test: trace one advertiser through ranking, click prediction, allocation, and payment. Then change only the quality score and say what moves. This checks whether you understand the platform mechanism as more than highest-bid-wins.
Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium: Self-test: after an observed action, write both the receiver's belief and the receiver's best response. Then mark whether the belief was pinned down by Bayes rule or chosen off path. This keeps belief discipline visible.
Signaling: Self-test: test whether the low type wants to imitate the high type's signal and whether the high type wants to separate. If both types prefer the same visible action, explain why the receiver should not infer separation.
Bargaining with Incomplete Information: Self-test: after a proposed offer, recalculate the set of types who accept. Then compare that selected group with the original population. If they differ, explain how the offer changed information as well as surplus.
Cheap Talk: Self-test: write the message each sender type would like to send, then ask what the receiver should infer. If all types send the same message, explain why the message pools information rather than revealing it. If messages differ, name the alignment that keeps them credible.
Common Knowledge: Self-test: construct a case where everyone privately knows the fact but no one knows whether everyone else knows. Then add a public announcement and explain which belief levels change. This tests the difference between truth and publicness.
